CHAPTER 5 — अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः (ATILOBHAH NA KARTAVYAH)

Introduction — शीर्षकस्य अर्थः (The meaning of the title)

The title of this lesson is a complete Sanskrit sentence: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः — 'excessive greed must not be indulged'. The word अतिलोभः is formed with the prefix अति (beyond, in excess) joined to लोभः (greed, grasping desire); grammatically it is a प्रादि-समास, glossed as लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः — desire that has crossed its proper limit. कर्तव्यः is a तव्यत्-कृदन्त from the root कृ (to do), meaning 'that which ought to be done'; with the negative न it means 'ought not to be done'. In classical Sanskrit ethics लोभ is counted among the षड्रिपवः, the six inner enemies of a human being — काम (desire), क्रोध (anger), लोभ (greed), मोह (delusion), मद (arrogance) and मात्सर्य (envy). Desire in itself keeps life moving; but when desire swells beyond need it becomes अतिलोभ, and the tradition warns that such greed destroys the greedy person before it destroys anyone else. This chapter (NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit, Course 309) teaches that warning through a famous public-domain fable from the पञ्चतन्त्र and through a set of सुभाषित verses contrasting लोभ (greed) with its remedy, सन्तोष (contentment).

कथा — लुब्धः जम्बुकः (The greedy jackal) — a Panchatantra fable retold in simple Sanskrit

पुरा कस्मिंश्चित् वने एकः व्याधः वसति स्म। एकदा सः मृगयार्थं धनुर्बाणं गृहीत्वा वनं गतः। तत्र सः एकं पुष्टं मृगं बाणेन हतवान्। ततः तं मृगं स्कन्धे कृत्वा गृहं प्रति चलितः।
Translation: Long ago, in a certain forest, there lived a hunter. One day, taking his bow and arrows, he went into the forest to hunt. There he killed a plump deer with an arrow, lifted it onto his shoulder and set off homeward.

मार्गे सः एकं महान्तं वराहं दृष्टवान्। व्याधः मृगं भूमौ निधाय तं वराहं बाणेन अताडयत्। क्रुद्धः वराहः अपि तीक्ष्णाभ्यां दंष्ट्राभ्यां व्याधम् अहन्। एवं व्याधः वराहः च उभौ अपि तत्र मृतौ। तयोः पादतले च एकः सर्पः अपि मर्दितः मृतः।
Translation: On the way he saw a huge wild boar. Setting the deer on the ground, the hunter struck the boar with an arrow; but the enraged boar gored the hunter with his sharp tusks. Thus both the hunter and the boar died on the spot — and a snake, crushed under their feet in the struggle, died as well.

ततः क्षुधार्तः एकः जम्बुकः आहारम् अन्विष्यन् तं प्रदेशम् आगच्छत्। सः मृतं व्याधं मृगं वराहं सर्पं च दृष्ट्वा परमप्रसन्नः अचिन्तयत् — 'अहो! मम भाग्यम्! अद्य महान् आहारराशिः प्राप्तः। एतत् भोजनं चिरकालं यापयिष्यामि।'
Translation: Then a jackal, tormented by hunger and searching for food, came to that spot. Seeing the dead hunter, the deer, the boar and the snake, he was overjoyed and thought: 'Ah, what luck! Today a great heap of food has come to me. I shall make this feast last a very long time.'

सः लुब्धः जम्बुकः एवम् अगणयत् —
मासमेकं नरो याति द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ ।
अहिरेकं दिनं याति अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः ॥
Translation of the jackal's calculation: 'The man will feed me for one month; the deer and the boar for two months; the snake will last one day. So today let me merely chew the bow-string (धनुर्गुणः) — that will be today's meal, and the rest will be saved.'

एवं विचिन्त्य सः धनुषः कोटौ बद्धं स्नायुनिर्मितं गुणं खादितुम् आरब्धवान्। छिन्ने गुणे आकुञ्चितं धनुः सहसा उत्प्लुत्य तस्य तालु भित्त्वा मस्तकं निर्भिद्य निर्गतम्। सः अतिलुब्धः जम्बुकः तत्क्षणम् एव मृतः।
Translation: Having reasoned thus, he began to gnaw the sinew-made string tied at the tip of the bow. The moment the string snapped, the bent bow sprang up violently, pierced his palate, burst through his head and came out. That over-greedy jackal died on the spot.

अतः एव उच्यते —
अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् ।
अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥
अन्वय: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः। लोभं न एव परित्यजेत्। अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य (जम्बुकस्य कृते) — धनुषा जम्बुकः हतः।
Translation: Excessive greed must not be indulged — though ordinary desire need not be abandoned altogether; (see what happened) — overcome by excessive greed, the jackal was slain by the bow.

शब्दार्थ (Word meanings from the story): व्याधः = hunter; मृगया = hunting; धनुः = bow; बाणः = arrow; मृगः = deer; स्कन्धः = shoulder; वराहः = boar; दंष्ट्रा = tusk, fang; सर्पः / अहिः = snake; क्षुधार्तः = tormented by hunger; जम्बुकः = jackal; आहारः = food; लुब्धः = greedy; मासः = month; धनुर्गुणः / ज्या = bow-string; स्नायुः = sinew; कोटिः = tip, end (of the bow); तालु = palate; मस्तकम् = head; हतः = killed; सन्तोषः = contentment; तृष्णा = craving.

नीतिः (The moral): The jackal stood before food enough for three months, yet died hungry — killed not by an enemy but by his own scheme of hoarding. Wanting to save everything, he chose the most worthless morsel, the bow-string, and the bow itself became the instrument of his death. The fable's irony is deliberate: greed does not merely fail to enrich us, it turns our own possessions into weapons against us. The wise course is मितभोगः — measured enjoyment — and सन्तोषः, contentment with what genuinely meets our need.

सुभाषितानि — Verses on लोभ and सन्तोष (with शब्दार्थ and अन्वय)

1) लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति लोभात् कामः प्रजायते ।
   लोभान्मोहश्च नाशश्च लोभः पापस्य कारणम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: लोभात् = from greed; क्रोधः = anger; प्रभवति = arises; कामः = desire; प्रजायते = is born; मोहः = delusion; नाशः = ruin, destruction; पापस्य = of sin; कारणम् = the cause.
   अन्वय: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति, लोभात् कामः प्रजायते, लोभात् मोहः च नाशः च (भवतः); लोभः पापस्य कारणम् (अस्ति)।
   Translation: From greed anger arises; from greed desire is born; from greed come delusion and ruin — greed is the root cause of sin.

2) सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां यत्सुखं शान्तचेतसाम् ।
   कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: सन्तोष-अमृत-तृप्तानाम् = of those satisfied by the nectar of contentment; यत् सुखम् = the happiness which; शान्तचेतसाम् = of those whose minds are at peace; कुतः = whence, how; तत् = that; धनलुब्धानाम् = of those greedy for wealth; इतः च इतः च = hither and thither; धावताम् = of those running.
   अन्वय: सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां शान्तचेतसां यत् सुखम् (अस्ति), तत् (सुखं) इतश्चेतश्च धावतां धनलुब्धानां कुतः?
   Translation: The happiness of the peaceful-minded, content as if filled with nectar — how can that happiness ever belong to the wealth-greedy who run restlessly here and there?

3) सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य सन्तुष्टं यस्य मानसम् ।
   उपानद्गूढपादस्य ननु चर्मावृतेव भूः ॥
   शब्दार्थ: सर्वाः सम्पत्तयः = all riches; तस्य = his; सन्तुष्टम् = contented; यस्य मानसम् = whose mind; उपानद्-गूढ-पादस्य = of one whose feet are covered by shoes; ननु = indeed; चर्म-आवृता इव = as if covered with leather; भूः = the earth.
   अन्वय: यस्य मानसं सन्तुष्टम्, तस्य सर्वाः सम्पत्तयः (सन्ति); उपानद्गूढपादस्य भूः ननु चर्मावृता इव (भवति)।
   Translation: He whose mind is contented owns all riches — just as, for a man whose feet are shod, the whole earth is as good as carpeted with leather.

4) यच्च कामसुखं लोके यच्च दिव्यं महत्सुखम् ।
   तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्यैते नार्हतः षोडशीं कलाम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: यत् च = and whatever; कामसुखम् = pleasure of desire; लोके = in the world; दिव्यम् = divine, heavenly; महत् सुखम् = great happiness; तृष्णा-क्षय-सुखस्य = of the happiness born of the destruction of craving; एते = these two; न अर्हतः = are not worth; षोडशीं कलाम् = a sixteenth part.
   अन्वय: लोके यत् च कामसुखम्, यत् च दिव्यं महत् सुखम् — एते (उभे) तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्य षोडशीं कलां न अर्हतः।
   Translation: Whatever pleasure desire gives in this world, and even the great bliss of heaven — the two together are not worth one-sixteenth of the happiness that comes when craving itself is extinguished.

5) The closing verse of the fable itself — अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् । अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥ — gathers the whole teaching: desire within limits is natural, but the one whom अतिलोभ overpowers is destroyed, as the jackal was slain by the very bow whose string he coveted.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the chapter

(A) सन्धिः (Sandhi). Examples drawn from the verses, with their सन्धि-विच्छेद:
  • लोभान्मोहः = लोभात् + मोहः — the final त् becomes न् before the nasal म् (व्यञ्जन-सन्धि).
  • नाशश्च = नाशः + च — visarga (ः) becomes श् before च (विसर्ग-सन्धि); likewise चेतश्च = चेतः + च.
  • कुतस्तत् = कुतः + तत् — visarga becomes स् before त्.
  • सुखस्यैते = सुखस्य + एते — अ + ए = ऐ (वृद्धि-सन्धि); compare वसुधा + एव = वसुधैव.
  • इतश्चेतश्च = इतः + च + इतः + च — first इतः + च → इतश्च; then the अ of च merges with the इ of the next इतः to give ए (गुण-सन्धि): इतश्चेतश्च, 'hither and thither'.
  • अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य = अतिलोभ + अभिभूतस्य — अ + अ = आ (दीर्घ-सन्धि)।

(B) समासः (Compounds):
  • अतिलोभः — प्रादि-समास: लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः, greed gone beyond limit.
  • शान्तचेतसाम् — बहुव्रीहि: शान्तं चेतः येषां ते शान्तचेतसः, 'those whose minds are at peace'.
  • धनलुब्धानाम् — सप्तमी-तत्पुरुष: धने लुब्धाः, 'greedy about wealth'.
  • सन्तोषामृतम् — कर्मधारय (रूपक): सन्तोषः एव अमृतम्, 'contentment which is itself nectar'.
  • धनुर्गुणः — षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष: धनुषः गुणः, 'the string of the bow'.

(C) विभक्तिः (Case endings) from the text:
  • पञ्चमी ('from'): लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति — anger arises FROM greed.
  • तृतीया ('by/with'): धनुषा हतः — slain BY the bow; बाणेन — with an arrow; दंष्ट्राभ्यां — with the two tusks.
  • षष्ठी ('of'): पापस्य कारणम् — the cause OF sin; धनुषः कोटिः — the tip OF the bow.
  • सप्तमी ('in/at'): लोके — in the world; भूमौ — on the ground; स्कन्धे — on the shoulder; मार्गे — on the way.
  • द्वितीया (object): मृगं हतवान्, लोभं न परित्यजेत्।

(D) कृदन्ताः and लकाराः:
  • कर्तव्यः — तव्यत्-कृदन्त from कृ: 'ought to be done'; similarly भक्ष्यः (यत्-कृदन्त from भक्ष्, 'fit to be eaten').
  • हतः, तृप्तः, मृतः, प्राप्तः — क्त-कृदन्त (past passive participles).
  • दृष्ट्वा, कृत्वा, गृहीत्वा — क्त्वा-प्रत्यय (having seen / done / taken); विचिन्त्य, भित्त्वा — the same sense (ल्यप् after a prefix in विचिन्त्य).
  • लट् लकार (present): प्रभवति, प्रजायते, याति, धावति।
  • लङ् लकार (past): अताडयत्, आगच्छत्, अचिन्तयत्।
  • विधिलिङ् (should/ought): परित्यजेत् — 'one should abandon'; compare ब्रूयात्।

सारांश (Summary)

In this chapter you studied the sentence-title अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः and its grammar; read the Panchatantra fable of the greedy jackal who, standing before months of food, chose to gnaw the bow-string to 'save' the rest and was killed by the springing bow; and memorised its closing verse अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो... You then studied four subhashitas: greed as the root of anger, desire, delusion, ruin and sin (लोभात् क्रोधः...); the unmatched happiness of the contented (सन्तोषामृततृप्तानाम्...); contentment as the possession of all riches, with the shoe-and-leather simile (सर्वाः सम्पत्तयः...); and the bliss of ending craving, worth more than all worldly and heavenly pleasure (तृष्णाक्षय...). Finally you drew grammar from the text: सन्धि splits such as लोभान्मोहः and इतश्चेतश्च, compounds such as अतिलोभः (प्रादि) and शान्तचेतस् (बहुव्रीहि), the cases पञ्चमी, तृतीया, षष्ठी and सप्तमी in use, and the forms कर्तव्यः (तव्यत्), हतः (क्त), दृष्ट्वा (क्त्वा) and परित्यजेत् (विधिलिङ्). The lesson of the jackal is timeless: greed beyond need destroys the greedy; contentment is the wealth that no one can take away.

topics.name: अतिलोभः — The Nature and Danger of Greed
topics.description: The meaning of the title अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः (excessive greed must not be indulged); लोभ as one of the six inner enemies (षड्रिपवः); the difference between natural desire and अतिलोभ; and why Sanskrit ethics treats greed as self-destructive.

topics.name: The Panchatantra Fable — The Greedy Jackal and the Bow
topics.description: The public-domain Panchatantra story of the hunter, deer, boar and snake who all perish, and the jackal who, out of greed to hoard the food, gnaws the bow-string first and is killed by the springing bow — ending in the verse अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यः।

topics.name: शब्दार्थ — Word Meanings and Vocabulary from the Story
topics.description: Key story and verse vocabulary with English meanings: व्याधः, मृगः, वराहः, जम्बुकः, धनुः, धनुर्गुणः, तालु, मस्तकम्, लुब्धः, तृष्णा, सन्तोषः and related words, and their use in sentences.

topics.name: Verses on लोभ and सन्तोष (Contentment)
topics.description: Four authentic subhashitas with शब्दार्थ, अन्वय and translation: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति...; सन्तोषामृततृप्तानाम्...; सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य...; and यच्च कामसुखं लोके... — contrasting the misery of greed with the happiness of contentment.

topics.name: व्याकरणम् — Sandhi, Samasa, Vibhakti and Verb Forms from the Text
topics.description: Grammar drawn from the chapter: सन्धि-विच्छेद of forms like लोभान्मोहः, नाशश्च, कुतस्तत्, सुखस्यैते and इतश्चेतश्च; compounds अतिलोभः (प्रादि), शान्तचेतस् (बहुव्रीहि), धनुर्गुणः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष); case usage (पञ्चमी, तृतीया, षष्ठी, सप्तमी); and forms कर्तव्यः (तव्यत्), हतः (क्त), दृष्ट्वा (क्त्वा), परित्यजेत् (विधिलिङ्)।

topics.name: Moral Application and Comprehension
topics.description: Translating the story and verses, drawing out the moral — greed turns our own possessions against us while contentment is unshakeable wealth — and applying the fable's lesson to modern situations such as hoarding, over-consumption and reckless pursuit of money.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: अतिलोभः — The Nature and Danger of Greed
learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning and grammar of the title अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः, distinguish natural desire from अतिलोभ, and describe लोभ's place among the six inner enemies (षड्रिपवः).

learning_outcomes.topic_name: The Panchatantra Fable — The Greedy Jackal and the Bow
learning_outcomes.description: Recall the sequence of events of the fable — the deaths of the hunter, deer, boar and snake, the jackal's calculation, and his death by the bow — and identify the characters and objects involved.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: The Panchatantra Fable — The Greedy Jackal and the Bow
learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning, irony and moral of the fable, including why the jackal chose the bow-string first and how his own hoarding scheme destroyed him.

learning_outcomes.topic_name: शब्दार्थ — Word Meanings and Vocabulary from the Story
learning_outcomes.description: Give the English शब्दार्थ of Sanskrit words drawn from the story and verses (व्याधः, वराहः, जम्बुकः, धनुर्गुणः, तालु, लुब्धः, तृष्णा, सन्तोषः etc.) and recognise them in context.
Analyse the subhashitas on लोभ and सन्तोष — give their अन्वय, शब्दार्थ and translation, and compare the chain of evils born of greed with the happiness of the contented.

chapter_summary.title: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Senior Secondary Sanskrit (309) summary covers Chapter 5: the sentence-title अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः ('excessive greed must not be indulged'), the Panchatantra fable of the greedy jackal killed by the bow whose string he coveted, four subhashitas contrasting लोभ with सन्तोष, and the grammar — सन्धि, समास, विभक्ति and verb forms — drawn from the text.

branches.label: शीर्षकम् — Title & Concept
details: लोभ is one of the six inner enemies (षड्रिपवः)

branches.label: कथा — The Jackal Fable
details: Hunter kills deer; boar kills hunter; both die; snake crushed
Jackal finds the feast, plans to hoard it for months
Chews the bow-string first to 'save' the rest
Bow springs, pierces his palate — the jackal dies

branches.label: सुभाषितानि — Verses
details: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति... लोभः पापस्य कारणम्
तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्य — worth more than all pleasures

branches.label: नीतिः — Moral
details: Greed turns our own possessions into weapons against us
Desire within need is natural; excess destroys
सन्तोष is the wealth no one can take away

sections.heading: The title and the idea of greed
bullets: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः is a full Sanskrit sentence: 'excessive greed must not be indulged'; अतिलोभः = अति (beyond) + लोभः (greed), a प्रादि-समास glossed लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः।
कर्तव्यः is a तव्यत्-कृदन्त of कृ ('ought to be done'); with न it expresses prohibition.
लोभ is one of the six inner enemies (षड्रिपवः): काम, क्रोध, लोभ, मोह, मद, मात्सर्य।
The chapter distinguishes natural desire, which sustains life, from अतिलोभ, which destroys the desirer himself.

sections.heading: The fable of the greedy jackal
bullets: A hunter kills a deer, then duels a boar: the boar's tusks kill the hunter, the arrow kills the boar, and a snake is crushed underfoot — four bodies lie together.
A starving jackal finds them and calculates: the man will last one month, deer and boar two months, the snake one day — मासमेकं नरो याति...
To 'save' all this food he decides to chew only the bow-string (धनुर्गुणः) today.
When the string snaps, the bent bow springs up, pierces his palate (तालु) and bursts through his head — he dies before eating anything.
The closing verse: अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् । अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥

sections.heading: Verses on greed and contentment
bullets: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति...: from greed spring anger, desire, delusion and ruin — greed is the root cause of sin (लोभः पापस्य कारणम्)।
सन्तोषामृततृप्तानाम्...: the peaceful-minded, filled with the nectar of contentment, enjoy a happiness the wealth-greedy — running hither and thither (इतश्चेतश्च) — can never taste.
सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य...: whoever's mind is content owns all riches, just as shod feet make the whole earth feel leather-covered.
यच्च कामसुखं लोके...: all worldly and even heavenly pleasure is not worth a sixteenth part (षोडशीं कलाम्) of the happiness of extinguished craving (तृष्णाक्षय)।

sections.heading: Sandhi and samasa from the text
bullets: लोभान्मोहः = लोभात् + मोहः (त् → न् before a nasal); नाशश्च = नाशः + च and चेतश्च = चेतः + च (विसर्ग → श्); कुतस्तत् = कुतः + तत् (विसर्ग → स्)।
सुखस्यैते = सुखस्य + एते (अ + ए = ऐ, वृद्धि-सन्धि); अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य = अतिलोभ + अभिभूतस्य (दीर्घ-सन्धि)।
इतश्चेतश्च = इतः + च + इतः + च — with गुण-सन्धि producing the ए — meaning 'hither and thither'.
समास: अतिलोभः (प्रादि), शान्तचेतस् (बहुव्रीहि: शान्तं चेतः येषाम्), धनलुब्ध (सप्तमी-तत्पुरुष), धनुर्गुणः (षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष), सन्तोषामृतम् (कर्मधारय-रूपक)।

sections.heading: Vibhakti and verb forms
bullets: पञ्चमी 'from': लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति; तृतीया 'by': धनुषा हतः, बाणेन; षष्ठी 'of': पापस्य कारणम्, धनुषः कोटिः; सप्तमी 'in': लोके, भूमौ, स्कन्धे।
कृदन्त forms: कर्तव्यः (तव्यत्), भक्ष्यः (यत्), हतः / तृप्तः / मृतः (क्त), दृष्ट्वा / कृत्वा (क्त्वा), विचिन्त्य (ल्यप्)।
लकाराः: लट् present (प्रभवति, याति, धावति), लङ् past (अताडयत्, अचिन्तयत्), विधिलिङ् 'should' (परित्यजेत्)।

key_takeaways: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः — greed beyond limit must not be indulged; ordinary desire within need is not condemned (लोभं नैव परित्यजेत्)।
The jackal died amid abundance: greed does not merely fail to enrich, it turns one's own possessions into instruments of ruin (धनुषा जम्बुको हतः)।
Greed is the root of a chain of evils — anger, desire, delusion, destruction — and the cause of sin: लोभः पापस्य कारणम्।
The contented mind owns all riches (सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य सन्तुष्टं यस्य मानसम्); the greedy run restlessly and never taste peace.
The happiness of ending craving (तृष्णाक्षय) outweighs every worldly and heavenly pleasure — not even a sixteenth part compares.
Grammar from the text: सन्धि-विच्छेद (लोभान्मोहः = लोभात् + मोहः), समास (अतिलोभः is प्रादि, शान्तचेतस् is बहुव्रीहि), and case usage (लोभात् पञ्चमी, धनुषा तृतीया)।
कर्तव्यः (तव्यत्-कृदन्त) and परित्यजेत् (विधिलिङ्) both express 'ought' — Sanskrit's grammar of duty frames the chapter's moral.

glossary.definition: Excessive greed; desire that has crossed its proper limit (अति + लोभः, a प्रादि-समास glossed लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः)।
'Ought to be done' — a तव्यत्-कृदन्त from the root कृ; with न it expresses what must not be done.
The six inner enemies of a person in Sanskrit ethics: काम, क्रोध, लोभ, मोह, मद and मात्सर्य।
A hunter; the man in the fable who kills the deer and is himself killed by the boar's tusks.
A jackal; the greedy protagonist of the fable, killed by the springing bow while gnawing its string.
A wild boar; the animal that gores the hunter with its tusks (दंष्ट्रा) and dies of the arrow-wound.
The bow-string (धनुषः गुणः, a षष्ठी-तत्पुरुष compound); also called ज्या; made of sinew (स्नायुः)।
The palate; the bow's tip pierced the jackal's palate and burst through his head when the string snapped.
Greedy, covetous; a क्त-type adjective describing the jackal (लुब्धः जम्बुकः) and the wealth-greedy (धनलुब्ध)।
Contentment; the remedy for greed — compared in the verses to nectar (सन्तोषामृतम्) and called the possession of all riches.
Craving, thirst for more; the verse says the happiness of its destruction (तृष्णाक्षय) surpasses all worldly and heavenly pleasure.
One whose mind is at peace — a बहुव्रीहि compound (शान्तं चेतः येषां ते); such people alone enjoy true happiness.
The prose word-order of a verse, arranging its words in natural sentence sequence to reveal the meaning.
Splitting a joined (sandhi) form back into its component words, e.g. लोभान्मोहः = लोभात् + मोहः।
The optative mood expressing 'should/ought', e.g. परित्यजेत् — 'one should abandon'.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः (NIOS Sanskrit 309, Chapter 5)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and give explanations in English. Refer to the fable and the verses in the lesson where needed.

questions.question:
Translate into simple English:
अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् ।
अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥
questions.answer: Excessive greed must not be indulged — though (ordinary) desire need not be abandoned altogether. (See what happened:) overcome by excessive greed, the jackal was slain by the bow. The verse closes the fable: the jackal who tried to hoard everything was killed by the very bow whose string he coveted.
questions.explanation: The verse balances two ideas: desire within limits is natural; desire beyond limits (अतिलोभ) destroys.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of each: व्याधः, वराहः, जम्बुकः, धनुर्गुणः, तालु.
questions.answer: व्याधः = hunter; वराहः = wild boar; जम्बुकः = jackal; धनुर्गुणः = bow-string; तालु = palate.
questions.explanation: All five words are central to the fable's action.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद (split) of: (a) लोभान्मोहः (b) नाशश्च.
questions.answer: (a) लोभान्मोहः = लोभात् + मोहः (final त् becomes न् before the nasal म्). (b) नाशश्च = नाशः + च (visarga ः becomes श् before च).
questions.explanation: Both forms occur in the verse लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति...

questions.question: State the विभक्ति and its meaning-role for each word: लोभात्, धनुषा, पापस्य.
questions.answer: लोभात् = पञ्चमी (ablative) → 'from greed'. धनुषा = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'by the bow'. पापस्य = षष्ठी (genitive) → 'of sin'.
questions.explanation: पञ्चमी shows source, तृतीया shows instrument, षष्ठी shows possession/relation.

questions.question: Narrate, in correct order, how the hunter, the boar and the snake died in the fable.
questions.answer: The hunter first killed a deer with an arrow. Carrying it home he met a huge boar and shot it; the wounded, enraged boar gored the hunter with its sharp tusks. Both the hunter and the boar died on the spot, and a snake, crushed under their feet in the struggle, also died.
questions.explanation: This sets the scene of four bodies — hunter, deer, boar, snake — that the jackal later finds.

questions.question: Explain the irony and the moral of the fable of the greedy jackal. Why did he choose the bow-string first, and what does his death teach? How can a student apply this lesson today?
questions.answer:
The irony: the jackal stood before food enough for three months, yet died without eating a morsel. Wanting to hoard everything, he calculated (the man one month, deer and boar two months, the snake one day) and chose the most worthless item, the bow-string, as 'today's meal' so that nothing valuable would be used up. When the string snapped, the bent bow sprang up, pierced his palate and killed him — his own hoarding scheme became the weapon of his death.
The moral: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः — greed beyond need destroys the greedy person himself; possessions grasped too tightly turn against their owner. Contentment and measured use (सन्तोष, मितभोग) are the wise course.
Application today: a student should avoid hoarding and over-accumulation — e.g. not sacrificing health, honesty or relationships to grab every advantage, mark or possession; spending and consuming within need; and remembering that peace of mind, not accumulation, is real wealth.
questions.explanation: Answer should cover the irony (death amid abundance), the mechanism (bow-string), the verse's teaching, and one or two modern applications.

questions.question: Write the अन्वय of the verse 'सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां यत्सुखं शान्तचेतसाम् । कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम् ॥' and explain its meaning in your own words.
questions.answer:
अन्वय: सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां शान्तचेतसां यत् सुखम् (अस्ति), तत् (सुखम्) इतश्चेतश्च धावतां धनलुब्धानां कुतः?
Meaning: Those whose minds are at peace, satisfied as if by the nectar of contentment, enjoy a special happiness. That happiness can never belong to the wealth-greedy, who run restlessly hither and thither (इतश्चेतश्च) chasing money. Contentment gives a settled, nectar-like joy; greed gives only endless running. The verse thus sets सन्तोष and लोभ as opposites: one fills the mind, the other empties it.
questions.explanation: Requires correct anvaya order plus a faithful prose explanation contrasting the contented and the greedy.

questions.question: Translate the jackal's calculation verse: 'मासमेकं नरो याति द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ । अहिरेकं दिनं याति अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः ॥' What flaw of character does it reveal?
questions.answer: Translation: 'The man will last (feed me) one month; the deer and the boar, two months; the snake will last one day; so today let the bow-string be my food.' The verse reveals the jackal's miserly, hoarding greed: even amid abundance he grudges himself proper food, choosing the most worthless morsel to 'save' the rest — the very calculation that kills him.
questions.explanation: भक्ष्यः is a यत्-कृदन्त, 'fit to be eaten'; the calculation is the heart of the fable's irony.

questions.question: Why is the chapter titled अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः and not merely लोभः न कर्तव्यः? Explain the force of अति.
questions.answer: The prefix अति means 'beyond, in excess'. The tradition does not condemn ordinary desire, which keeps life moving — the verse itself says लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् (desire need not be wholly abandoned). What is forbidden is desire that crosses its proper limit — अतिलोभ. The title therefore precisely targets excessive greed, not desire as such.
questions.explanation: अतिलोभः is a प्रादि-समास: लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः।

questions.question: Identify the grammatical form of each and state its sense: कर्तव्यः, दृष्ट्वा, परित्यजेत्.
questions.answer: कर्तव्यः — तव्यत्-कृदन्त from कृ, meaning 'ought to be done'. दृष्ट्वा — क्त्वा-प्रत्यय form from दृश्, meaning 'having seen'. परित्यजेत् — विधिलिङ् (optative) of परि + त्यज्, meaning 'one should abandon'.
questions.explanation: All three forms carry the chapter's grammar of duty and sequence.

questions.question: The word 'अतिलोभः' is formed from the prefix अति + ____.
questions.explanation: अति (beyond, in excess) + लोभः (greed) = excessive greed; a प्रादि-समास।

questions.question: The title 'अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः' means
options: excessive greed must not be indulged
questions.answer: excessive greed must not be indulged
questions.explanation: कर्तव्यः = 'ought to be done'; with न it prohibits — greed beyond limit must not be practised.

questions.question: The prefix 'अति' in अतिलोभः conveys the sense of
questions.explanation: अति = beyond/excessive; अतिलोभः is desire that has crossed its proper limit (लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः)।

questions.question: In Sanskrit ethics, लोभ is counted among the
questions.explanation: The six inner enemies are काम, क्रोध, लोभ, मोह, मद and मात्सर्य।

questions.question: According to the chapter, अतिलोभ differs from ordinary desire because it is
options: desire swollen beyond one's genuine need
questions.answer: desire swollen beyond one's genuine need
questions.explanation: The verse says लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् — ordinary desire is natural; excess (अति) is what destroys.

questions.question: The fable of the greedy jackal in this chapter comes from which classical text tradition?
questions.explanation: The jackal-and-bow story is a famous public-domain Panchatantra fable, also found in the Hitopadesha tradition.

questions.question: According to the chapter, the true remedy for लोभ is
questions.explanation: The subhashitas contrast greed with सन्तोष, the nectar-like contentment of the peaceful-minded.

questions.question: In the title, the word कर्तव्यः together with न expresses
options: prohibition — what ought not to be done
questions.answer: prohibition — what ought not to be done
questions.explanation: कर्तव्यः (तव्यत्-कृदन्त) means 'ought to be done'; न कर्तव्यः = must not be done.

questions.question: Who went into the forest to hunt at the beginning of the fable?
questions.explanation: The story opens: कस्मिंश्चित् वने एकः व्याधः... मृगयार्थं वनं गतः।

questions.question: The first animal the hunter killed with his arrow was a
questions.explanation: He killed a plump deer, lifted it onto his shoulder and set off home.

questions.question: Which animal attacked and killed the hunter on his way home?
questions.explanation: The wounded boar gored the hunter with its sharp tusks (तीक्ष्णाभ्यां दंष्ट्राभ्याम्)।

questions.question: Which small creature also died, crushed underfoot during the fight?
questions.explanation: तयोः पादतले एकः सर्पः अपि मर्दितः मृतः — a snake was trampled in the struggle.

questions.question: Who arrived at the spot and found the four dead bodies?
questions.explanation: क्षुधार्तः जम्बुकः आहारम् अन्विष्यन् तं प्रदेशम् आगच्छत्।

questions.question: What did the jackal decide to eat first?
questions.explanation: His verse ends: अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः — 'today let the bow-string be my food.'

questions.question: Why did the jackal choose to gnaw the bow-string first?
options: to save the valuable meat for the coming months
because the string was the tastiest part
because he feared the hunter would wake
questions.answer: to save the valuable meat for the coming months
questions.explanation: Out of hoarding greed he grudged himself proper food and picked the most worthless morsel first.

questions.question: How did the jackal die?
options: the bow-tip sprang up and pierced his palate
he choked on the deer's bone
questions.answer: the bow-tip sprang up and pierced his palate
questions.explanation: छिन्ने गुणे धनुः उत्प्लुत्य तस्य तालु भित्त्वा मस्तकं निर्भिद्य निर्गतम् — the released bow burst through his head.

questions.question: In the jackal's calculation verse, the man's body would feed him for
questions.explanation: मासमेकं नरो याति — 'the man will last one month.'

questions.question: According to the jackal's verse, the deer and the boar together would last
questions.explanation: द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ — the deer and boar (मृग-सूकरौ) would feed him two months.

questions.question: In the jackal's calculation, the snake (अहिः) would last
questions.explanation: अहिरेकं दिनं याति — 'the snake will last one day.'

questions.question: The bow-string that the jackal gnawed was made of
questions.explanation: The story says स्नायुनिर्मितं गुणम् — a string made of sinew, which is why it tempted the jackal as food.

questions.question: The moral of the jackal fable is best stated as
options: excessive greed destroys the greedy person himself
meat should always be eaten fresh
questions.answer: excessive greed destroys the greedy person himself
questions.explanation: The closing verse states it: अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः।

questions.question: Complete the verse: अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा ____ हतः ।
questions.explanation: 'Overcome by excessive greed, the jackal was slain by the bow.'

questions.question: In the fable, the jackal stands as a symbol of
options: a person ruined by hoarding greed
questions.answer: a person ruined by hoarding greed
questions.explanation: The fable is a नीतिकथा: each character embodies a human quality — the jackal embodies अतिलोभ।

questions.question: The central irony of the fable is that the jackal
options: died hungry in the midst of abundant food
never found any food at all
ate too much and fell sick
questions.answer: died hungry in the midst of abundant food
questions.explanation: Food for three months lay before him, yet his hoarding scheme killed him before he ate anything.

questions.question: In the verse ending the fable, 'लोभं नैव परित्यजेत्' teaches that
options: ordinary desire need not be abandoned altogether — only its excess
all desire must be destroyed immediately
questions.answer: ordinary desire need not be abandoned altogether — only its excess
questions.explanation: The verse balances the teaching: desire within need is natural; अतिलोभ alone is condemned.

questions.question: The bow in the fable functions as a symbol of how
options: one's own hoarded possessions can become the instrument of one's ruin
questions.answer: one's own hoarded possessions can become the instrument of one's ruin
questions.explanation: The jackal was killed not by an enemy but by an object he was 'saving' — greed turns possessions into weapons.

questions.question: The jackal's real mistake, according to the chapter, was
options: miserly hoarding — grudging himself proper food to save everything
questions.answer: miserly hoarding — grudging himself proper food to save everything
questions.explanation: His plan to stretch the food over months made him pick the worthless bow-string — the fatal choice.

questions.question: Which quality, had the jackal possessed it, would have saved his life?
options: सन्तोषः — contentment with what meets the need
questions.answer: सन्तोषः — contentment with what meets the need
questions.explanation: Had he simply eaten what he needed, the bow would never have touched him.

questions.question: A story like this one, in which animals act out a moral teaching, is called in Sanskrit a
questions.explanation: The Panchatantra is a collection of नीतिकथा — fables that teach worldly wisdom and ethics.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'व्याधः' means
questions.explanation: व्याधः = hunter; he is the first character of the fable.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'जम्बुकः' means
questions.explanation: जम्बुकः (also शृगालः) = jackal, the greedy protagonist.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'वराहः' means
questions.explanation: वराहः = boar; also called सूकरः in the jackal's verse (मृगसूकरौ)।

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'धनुः' means
questions.explanation: धनुः = bow; its string is धनुर्गुणः or ज्या।

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'धनुर्गुणः' means
questions.explanation: धनुषः गुणः = the string of the bow (also called ज्या), made of sinew.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'तालु' means
questions.explanation: तालु = palate; the bow-tip pierced the jackal's palate (तालु भित्त्वा)।

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'क्षुधार्तः' means
questions.explanation: क्षुधा (hunger) + आर्तः (afflicted) = hunger-stricken; the jackal's state on arrival.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'आहारः' means
questions.explanation: आहारः = food; the jackal rejoiced at the महान् आहारराशिः (great heap of food).

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'हतः' means
questions.explanation: हतः is the क्त-participle of हन् (to kill): धनुषा जम्बुको हतः — the jackal was killed by the bow.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'लुब्धः' means
questions.explanation: लुब्धः = greedy/covetous; hence धनलुब्धाः = those greedy for wealth.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'तृष्णा' means
questions.explanation: तृष्णा = craving; the verse praises तृष्णाक्षय — the extinction of craving.

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'सन्तोषः' means
questions.explanation: सन्तोषः = contentment — the chapter's remedy for greed, compared to nectar (अमृतम्)।

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'मस्तकम्' means
questions.explanation: मस्तकम् = head; the bow-tip burst through the jackal's head (मस्तकं निर्भिद्य)।

questions.question: शब्दार्थ: 'दंष्ट्रा' means
questions.explanation: दंष्ट्रा = tusk/fang; the boar killed the hunter तीक्ष्णाभ्यां दंष्ट्राभ्याम् — with his two sharp tusks.

questions.question: In the jackal's verse, 'अहिः' is a synonym for
questions.explanation: अहिः = snake; अहिरेकं दिनं याति — 'the snake will last one day.'

questions.question: Complete the verse: लोभात् क्रोधः ____ ।
questions.explanation: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति — 'from greed anger arises.'

questions.question: According to the verse, लोभः is the कारणम् (cause) of
questions.explanation: लोभः पापस्य कारणम् — greed is the root cause of sin.

questions.question: According to 'लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति...', which set of evils springs from greed?
questions.explanation: The verse lists anger, desire, delusion and ruin as offspring of greed.

questions.question: In 'सन्तोषामृततृप्तानाम्', contentment is compared to
questions.explanation: सन्तोष-अमृत = the nectar of contentment, which fully satisfies the peaceful-minded.

questions.question: In the same verse, the wealth-greedy (धनलुब्धाः) are described as
options: running restlessly hither and thither (इतश्चेतश्च धावताम्)
questions.answer: running restlessly hither and thither (इतश्चेतश्च धावताम्)
questions.explanation: The greedy chase wealth in all directions and so never taste the happiness of the contented.

questions.question: According to 'सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य...', who possesses all riches?
options: the one whose mind is contented (सन्तुष्टं यस्य मानसम्)
the one who owns the most gold
the one who rules a kingdom
questions.answer: the one whose mind is contented (सन्तुष्टं यस्य मानसम्)
questions.explanation: Contentment itself is the possession of all wealth — the verse's central claim.

questions.question: The simile 'उपानद्गूढपादस्य ननु चर्मावृतेव भूः' means
options: for one whose feet are shod, the whole earth is as if covered with leather
one should always walk barefoot on leather
the earth is truly made of leather
shoes must be removed before walking
questions.answer: for one whose feet are shod, the whole earth is as if covered with leather
questions.explanation: Just as shoes make every road smooth, contentment makes every circumstance feel rich.

questions.question: According to 'यच्च कामसुखं लोके...', worldly and heavenly pleasures together are not worth what fraction of the bliss of ending craving?
questions.explanation: तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्यैते नार्हतः षोडशीं कलाम् — not worth one-sixteenth of the happiness of extinguished craving.

questions.question: In the verse, 'शान्तचेतसाम्' means
options: of those whose minds are at peace
of those who live in forests
questions.answer: of those whose minds are at peace
questions.explanation: शान्तं चेतः येषां ते शान्तचेतसः — a बहुव्रीहि compound: the peaceful-minded.

questions.question: Which verse of the chapter is spoken by the jackal himself?
options: मासमेकं नरो याति द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ...
questions.answer: मासमेकं नरो याति द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ...
questions.explanation: It is the jackal's hoarding calculation: man one month, deer and boar two months, snake one day.

questions.question: 'अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः' — the force of the यत्-कृदन्त भक्ष्यः here is
options: 'is to be eaten' — today the bow-string is the thing fit to be eaten
'was eaten' — the string had already been eaten
'will feed' — the string will feed others
questions.answer: 'is to be eaten' — today the bow-string is the thing fit to be eaten
questions.explanation: भक्ष्यः (from भक्ष्) is a potential participle: 'fit/due to be eaten' — the jackal assigns today's ration.

questions.question: सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'लोभान्मोहः' is
questions.explanation: The final त् of लोभात् becomes न् before the nasal म् (व्यञ्जन-सन्धि)।

questions.question: सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'नाशश्च' is
questions.explanation: Visarga (ः) becomes श् before च — विसर्ग-सन्धि, as also in चेतश्च = चेतः + च।

questions.question: सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'कुतस्तत्' is
questions.explanation: Visarga becomes स् before त् — कुतः + तत् = कुतस्तत्।

questions.question: The sandhi in 'सुखस्यैते' (सुखस्य + एते) is
questions.explanation: अ + ए = ऐ is वृद्धि-सन्धि, exactly as in वसुधा + एव = वसुधैव।

questions.question: The full split of 'इतश्चेतश्च' is
questions.explanation: इतः + च → इतश्च; then the अ of च merges with the इ of the next इतः (गुण-सन्धि) — 'hither and thither'.

questions.question: The compound 'अतिलोभः' is an example of which समास?
questions.explanation: A prefix (अति) compounded with a noun: लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः — greed gone beyond limit.

questions.question: 'शान्तचेतसाम्' (शान्तं चेतः येषां ते) is which समास?
questions.explanation: The compound denotes a third thing — persons WHOSE minds are at peace — the mark of बहुव्रीहि।

questions.question: 'धनुर्गुणः', glossed धनुषः गुणः ('the string OF the bow'), is which समास?
questions.explanation: The first member stands in the genitive (षष्ठी) relation to the second: धनुषः गुणः।

questions.question: In 'लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति', the word लोभात् is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: Anger arises FROM greed — source is expressed by पञ्चमी।

questions.question: In 'धनुषा जम्बुको हतः', the word धनुषा is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: The jackal was slain BY the bow — the instrument takes तृतीया।

questions.question: In 'लोभः पापस्य कारणम्', the word पापस्य is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: Greed is the cause OF sin — the relation 'of' takes षष्ठी।

questions.question: In 'यच्च कामसुखं लोके', the word लोके is in which विभक्ति?
questions.explanation: 'IN the world' — place is expressed by सप्तमी: लोके।

questions.question: कर्तव्यः ('ought to be done') is formed with which कृदन्त suffix?
questions.explanation: कृ + तव्यत् = कर्तव्य — the gerundive of obligation; similarly पठितव्यम्, वक्तव्यम्।

questions.question: हतः, तृप्तः and मृतः are all examples of which participle?
questions.explanation: क्त-कृदन्त gives the sense 'killed / satisfied / dead' — completed action.

questions.question: परित्यजेत् ('one should abandon') is in which लकार?
questions.explanation: The -एत् ending marks विधिलिङ्, expressing 'should/ought' — as in ब्रूयात्।

questions.question: प्रभवति and प्रजायते, as used in the verse, are in which लकार?
questions.explanation: General truths are stated in the present: 'anger ARISES from greed'.

questions.question: The best English rendering of 'अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत्' is
options: excessive greed must not be indulged, though desire need not be wholly abandoned
greed and desire must both be totally destroyed
greed should be practised but hidden
desire is excessive only in animals
questions.answer: excessive greed must not be indulged, though desire need not be wholly abandoned
questions.explanation: The verse condemns excess, not desire itself — a balanced senior-secondary reading.

questions.question: Which modern situation most closely repeats the jackal's mistake?
options: a person who hoards essential goods to profiteer and loses everything when the scheme collapses
a student who revises daily for an examination
a farmer who stores seed grain for next season
a doctor who saves a patient's life
questions.answer: a person who hoards essential goods to profiteer and loses everything when the scheme collapses
questions.explanation: Hoarding beyond need, at the cost of present good sense, is exactly the jackal's अतिलोभ; prudent storing for genuine need is not.

questions.question: Which behaviour best shows सन्तोष as the chapter teaches it?
options: using what one needs, enjoying it fully, and not grasping for excess
refusing to eat anything at all
questions.answer: using what one needs, enjoying it fully, and not grasping for excess
questions.explanation: सन्तोष is measured enjoyment (मितभोग), not self-starvation and not hoarding.

questions.question: A student keeps buying gadgets she never uses, chasing each new release. Which verse of the chapter most directly diagnoses her state?
options: कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम् — the greedy run restlessly and find no happiness
मासमेकं नरो याति — the man lasts one month
अहिरेकं दिनं याति — the snake lasts one day
द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ — the deer and boar last two months
questions.answer: कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम् — the greedy run restlessly and find no happiness
questions.explanation: Restless acquisition without satisfaction is exactly the इतश्चेतश्च धावताम् of the wealth-greedy.

questions.question: True or False: The jackal died when the bow-tip sprang up and pierced his palate.
questions.explanation: छिन्ने गुणे धनुः उत्प्लुत्य तस्य तालु भित्त्वा... — the released bow killed him instantly.

questions.question: True or False: The hunter in the fable was killed by the snake.
questions.explanation: The hunter was gored by the boar's tusks; the snake was crushed underfoot and died.

questions.question: True or False: अतिलोभः is a प्रादि-समास (prefix अति + लोभः).
questions.explanation: It is glossed लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः — greed gone beyond its limit.

questions.question: True or False: In 'लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति', the word लोभात् is in तृतीया विभक्ति.
questions.explanation: लोभात् is पञ्चमी (ablative) — anger arises FROM greed; तृतीया would be लोभेन।

questions.question: True or False: The verse सन्तोषामृततृप्तानाम्... praises the happiness of the greedy.
questions.explanation: It praises the contented and peaceful-minded; the greedy, running hither and thither, can never share that happiness.

questions.question: True or False: The fable of the greedy jackal belongs to the public-domain Panchatantra tradition.
questions.explanation: It is a classical Panchatantra fable, retold in simple Sanskrit in this lesson.

questions.question: True or False: The Sanskrit word जम्बुकः means 'boar'.
questions.explanation: जम्बुकः = jackal; the boar is वराहः (or सूकरः)।

questions.question: True or False: परित्यजेत् is a विधिलिङ् (optative) form meaning 'one should abandon'.
questions.explanation: The -एत् ending marks the optative of obligation/advice.

questions.question: True or False: According to the verse, greed is the cause of sin (लोभः पापस्य कारणम्).
questions.explanation: The verse traces anger, desire, delusion and ruin — and sin itself — back to greed.

questions.question: True or False: The jackal planned to eat the deer's flesh first and the bow-string last.
questions.explanation: It was the reverse: to save the meat he chose the bow-string as today's food — the choice that killed him.

questions.question: Complete the title of the chapter: अतिलोभः न ________ ।
questions.explanation: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः — excessive greed must not be indulged.

questions.question: Complete the verse: अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा ________ हतः ।
questions.explanation: Overcome by excessive greed, the JACKAL was slain by the bow.

questions.question: Complete the verse: लोभात् ________ प्रभवति ।
questions.explanation: From greed ANGER arises — the first link of the verse's chain of evils.

questions.question: Complete the verse: लोभः ________ कारणम् ।
questions.explanation: Greed is the cause OF SIN — पापस्य is षष्ठी विभक्ति।

questions.question: The Sanskrit word for 'hunter', the first character of the fable, is ________ .
questions.explanation: व्याधः = hunter; he went to the forest मृगयार्थम् (for hunting).

questions.question: The Sanskrit word for 'bow' (the weapon that finally killed the jackal) is ________ .
questions.explanation: धनुः = bow; its string is धनुर्गुणः।

questions.question: To save the meat, the jackal decided first to gnaw the ________ (Sanskrit word for bow-string, from his verse अद्य भक्ष्यो...).
questions.explanation: अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः — 'today the bow-string is to be eaten.'

questions.question: Complete the verse: सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां यत्सुखं ________ ।
questions.explanation: The happiness of the peaceful-minded (शान्तचेतसाम्), content with the nectar of contentment.

questions.question: Complete the verse: सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य सन्तुष्टं यस्य ________ ।
questions.explanation: He whose MIND (मानसम्) is contented owns all riches.

questions.question: सन्धि-विच्छेद: नाशश्च = नाशः + ________ ।
questions.explanation: Visarga becomes श् before च: नाशः + च = नाशश्च।

questions.question: सन्धि-विच्छेद: लोभान्मोहः = ________ + मोहः ।
questions.explanation: The final त् of लोभात् becomes न् before the nasal म्।

questions.question: कर्तव्यः is formed from the root कृ with the कृदन्त suffix ________ .
questions.explanation: कृ + तव्यत् = कर्तव्य, 'ought to be done' — the gerundive of obligation.

questions.question: Complete the jackal's verse: मासमेकं नरो ________ द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ ।
questions.explanation: मासमेकं नरो याति — 'the man will last one month.'

questions.question: The Sanskrit word for 'contentment', the chapter's remedy for greed, is ________ .
questions.explanation: सन्तोषः = contentment, compared in the verse to nectar (सन्तोषामृतम्)।

questions.question: Complete the jackal's verse: अहिरेकं ________ याति अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः ।
questions.explanation: अहिरेकं दिनं याति — 'the snake will last one day.'

questions.question: Explain the meaning of the chapter title अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः, analysing both its words.
questions.answer: अतिलोभः = अति (beyond, in excess) + लोभः (greed) — greed that has crossed its proper limit (a प्रादि-समास, glossed लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः). कर्तव्यः is a तव्यत्-कृदन्त of कृ meaning 'ought to be done'; with न it prohibits. The title therefore means: 'Excessive greed must not be indulged.'
questions.explanation: Both the compound and the gerundive must be identified for full marks.

questions.question: List, in order, the four beings the jackal found dead, and state how each died.
questions.answer: (1) The deer (मृगः) — shot by the hunter's arrow. (2) The hunter (व्याधः) — gored by the boar's sharp tusks. (3) The boar (वराहः) — killed by the hunter's arrow. (4) The snake (सर्पः) — crushed underfoot during the fight.
questions.explanation: The four bodies together form the 'heap of food' that tempts the jackal.

questions.question: Why did the jackal not eat the meat immediately, though he was starving?
questions.answer: Out of hoarding greed he wanted the food to last for months. He calculated that the man would feed him one month, the deer and boar two months and the snake one day, and decided to spend today on the most worthless morsel — the bow-string — so that nothing valuable would be used up.
questions.explanation: His postponement of enjoyment out of greed is the fable's central irony.

questions.question: Describe exactly how the jackal died.
questions.answer: He began gnawing the sinew string tied at the bow's tip. The moment the string snapped, the bent bow straightened violently and sprang up; its tip pierced his palate (तालु), burst through his head (मस्तकम्) and came out. He died on the spot.
questions.explanation: छिन्ने गुणे धनुः उत्प्लुत्य तालु भित्त्वा मस्तकं निर्भिद्य निर्गतम्।

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of: मृगया, स्कन्धः, दंष्ट्रा, कोटिः.
questions.answer: मृगया = hunting; स्कन्धः = shoulder; दंष्ट्रा = tusk/fang; कोटिः = tip or end (of the bow).
questions.explanation: All four occur in the narrative of the hunter and the bow.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: सन्तोषः, तृष्णा, लुब्धः, स्नायुः.
questions.answer: सन्तोषः = contentment; तृष्णा = craving, thirst for more; लुब्धः = greedy; स्नायुः = sinew (of which the bow-string was made).
questions.explanation: These words carry the chapter's moral vocabulary.

questions.question: Translate into English: अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् ।
questions.answer: Excessive greed must not be indulged — (yet) one need not abandon desire altogether. The line condemns only desire that crosses its limit, not natural desire itself.
questions.explanation: The double statement balances prohibition of excess with acceptance of natural desire.

questions.question: Write the अन्वय of: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति लोभात् कामः प्रजायते । लोभान्मोहश्च नाशश्च लोभः पापस्य कारणम् ॥
questions.answer: अन्वय: लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति। लोभात् कामः प्रजायते। लोभात् मोहः च नाशः च (भवतः)। लोभः पापस्य कारणम् (अस्ति)। — From greed anger arises, from greed desire is born, from greed come delusion and ruin; greed is the cause of sin.
questions.explanation: The anvaya resolves the sandhi लोभान्मोहश्च into लोभात् मोहः च।

questions.question: Translate into English: सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां यत्सुखं शान्तचेतसाम् । कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम् ॥
questions.answer: The happiness enjoyed by the peaceful-minded, satisfied by the nectar of contentment — how can that happiness ever belong to those greedy for wealth, who keep running hither and thither? Contentment gives a settled joy that restless greed can never obtain.
questions.explanation: इतश्चेतश्च धावताम् = 'of those running here and there' — the restlessness of greed.

questions.question: Explain the simile in: उपानद्गूढपादस्य ननु चर्मावृतेव भूः.
questions.answer: For a man whose feet are covered by shoes (उपानद्गूढपाद), the whole earth feels as if carpeted with leather — he need not pave the world, only cover his own feet. Likewise, one who covers his own mind with contentment finds every circumstance rich; he need not acquire everything outside.
questions.explanation: The simile argues that inner contentment, not outer accumulation, transforms one's whole world.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of: (a) कुतस्तत् (b) चेतश्च.
questions.answer: (a) कुतस्तत् = कुतः + तत् — visarga becomes स् before त्. (b) चेतश्च = चेतः + च — visarga becomes श् before च.
questions.explanation: Both are विसर्ग-सन्धि forms from the verse कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानाम्...।

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of: (a) सुखस्यैते (b) अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य, naming the sandhi in each.
questions.answer: (a) सुखस्यैते = सुखस्य + एते; अ + ए = ऐ, so it is वृद्धि-सन्धि. (b) अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य = अतिलोभ + अभिभूतस्य; अ + अ = आ, so it is दीर्घ-सन्धि.
questions.explanation: Compare वसुधा + एव = वसुधैव (वृद्धि) and न + अस्ति = नास्ति (दीर्घ)।

questions.question: Name the समास and give the विग्रह (analysis) of: (a) अतिलोभः (b) शान्तचेतस्.
questions.answer: (a) अतिलोभः — प्रादि-समास; विग्रह: लोभम् अतिक्रान्तः, 'greed gone beyond limit'. (b) शान्तचेतस् — बहुव्रीहि; विग्रह: शान्तं चेतः येषां ते, 'those whose minds are at peace'.
questions.explanation: बहुव्रीहि denotes a possessor outside the compound's own members.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति and meaning-role of each: धनुषा, लोभात्, लोके, पापस्य.
questions.answer: धनुषा = तृतीया, 'by the bow' (instrument). लोभात् = पञ्चमी, 'from greed' (source). लोके = सप्तमी, 'in the world' (location). पापस्य = षष्ठी, 'of sin' (relation).
questions.explanation: Four of the chapter's key case-forms in one set.

questions.question: Explain the form कर्तव्यः and give two more words formed with the same suffix.
questions.answer: कर्तव्यः = कृ + तव्यत्, a gerundive (कृदन्त) meaning 'ought to be done'. Other तव्यत् forms: पठितव्यम् ('ought to be read'), वक्तव्यम् ('ought to be said') — likewise दातव्यम्, श्रोतव्यम्.
questions.explanation: Any two correct तव्यत् forms earn the second mark.

questions.question: Identify the लकार (or form) of each verb: प्रभवति, परित्यजेत्, अताडयत्, दृष्ट्वा.
questions.answer: प्रभवति — लट् (present, 'arises'). परित्यजेत् — विधिलिङ् (optative, 'should abandon'). अताडयत् — लङ् (past, 'struck'). दृष्ट्वा — not a लकार but a क्त्वा-प्रत्यय indeclinable, 'having seen'.
questions.explanation: The last item tests that students distinguish participles from finite लकार forms.

questions.question: State the moral of the fable in two or three sentences.
questions.answer: Greed beyond need destroys the greedy person himself. The jackal, surrounded by months of food, died without eating a morsel because his hoarding scheme led him to gnaw the fatal bow-string. Contentment and measured enjoyment, not accumulation, are the wise course — अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः।
questions.explanation: The answer should mention both the irony and the positive teaching (सन्तोष/मितभोग)।

questions.question: Translate the jackal's calculation verse: मासमेकं नरो याति द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ । अहिरेकं दिनं याति अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः ॥
questions.answer: 'The man will last me one month; the deer and the boar, two months; the snake will last one day; so today let the bow-string be my food.' The jackal rations the feast to stretch it as long as possible.
questions.explanation: मृगसूकरौ is a द्वन्द्व (deer and boar); भक्ष्यः = 'to be eaten' (यत्-कृदन्त)।

questions.question: Give one modern example of अतिलोभ and state which detail of the fable it matches.
questions.answer: Example: an investor who, not content with good profit, stakes everything on ever riskier schemes and loses all — like the jackal who, not content with abundant meat, grasped at the bow-string too and lost his life. (Any parallel example — hoarding goods, over-consumption, endless overtime ruining health — with a matching fable detail is acceptable.)
questions.explanation: The point of correspondence: the greedy act turns one's own assets into the instrument of loss.

questions.question: Distinguish लोभ from सन्तोष as this chapter presents them.
questions.answer: लोभ is the grasping thirst for more than one needs; it breeds anger, delusion and ruin, keeps a person running restlessly (इतश्चेतश्च) and, in excess, destroys him. सन्तोष is contentment with what genuinely meets one's need; it is compared to nectar, gives settled happiness, and makes its possessor rich in every circumstance.
questions.explanation: The two terms anchor the opposite poles of the chapter's teaching.

questions.question: Why does the verse call लोभ 'पापस्य कारणम्' — the cause of sin? Argue from its own chain of effects.
questions.answer: The verse derives every named evil from greed: anger (क्रोध) when greed is blocked, desire (काम) when it is fed, delusion (मोह) when it clouds judgement, and ruin (नाश) when it acts. Since these are the states in which people commit wrongs, greed stands at the root of them all — hence लोभः पापस्य कारणम्।
questions.explanation: A senior-secondary answer should connect each named evil back to greed as the common root.

questions.question: Name the six inner enemies (षड्रिपवः) of Sanskrit ethics, and state which one this chapter targets.
questions.answer: The षड्रिपवः are काम (desire), क्रोध (anger), लोभ (greed), मोह (delusion), मद (arrogance) and मात्सर्य (envy). This chapter targets लोभ — specifically its excess, अतिलोभ।
questions.explanation: The chapter's verse also shows लोभ generating काम, क्रोध and मोह — making it the most dangerous of the six.

questions.question: Retell the complete fable of the greedy jackal in English, in correct sequence, and end with its moral verse and meaning.
questions.answer: A hunter went to the forest, killed a plump deer with an arrow and carried it homeward on his shoulder. On the way a huge boar appeared; the hunter shot it, but the enraged boar gored him with its sharp tusks. Both died on the spot, and a snake crushed under their feet died too. A starving jackal then arrived and rejoiced at the heap of food. Calculating that the man would feed him one month, the deer and boar two months and the snake one day, he decided to 'save' it all and chew only the bow-string today. As he gnawed the sinew string it snapped; the bent bow sprang up, pierced his palate, burst through his head, and he died instantly. The moral verse: अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् । अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥ — excessive greed must not be indulged (though desire need not be wholly abandoned); overcome by excessive greed, the jackal was slain by the bow.
questions.explanation: Full marks require correct sequence (deer, hunter-boar duel, snake, jackal, bow-string, death) plus the verse and its meaning.

questions.question: Explain fully the verse: अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् । अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥ Give its अन्वय, key शब्दार्थ, translation and teaching.
questions.answer: अन्वय: अतिलोभः न कर्तव्यः। लोभं न एव परित्यजेत्। अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य — धनुषा जम्बुकः हतः। शब्दार्थ: अतिलोभः = excessive greed; कर्तव्यः = ought to be done (तव्यत्-कृदन्त); परित्यजेत् = should abandon (विधिलिङ्); अभिभूतस्य = of one overcome; धनुषा = by the bow (तृतीया); हतः = killed (क्त). Translation: Excessive greed must not be indulged — yet desire need not be abandoned altogether; (for see:) overcome by excessive greed, the jackal was slain by the bow. Teaching: the verse is the fable's own summary — natural desire keeps life moving, but desire beyond limit destroys the desirer, turning even his 'saved' possessions into weapons against him.
questions.explanation: Anvaya, at least four shabdartha items, translation and the balanced teaching are all expected.

questions.question: 'सन्तोष is the true wealth.' Evaluate this claim using at least two verses from the chapter, and state your own reasoned conclusion.
questions.answer: Two verses argue the claim directly. (1) सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य सन्तुष्टं यस्य मानसम् — whoever's mind is content owns all riches, as one with shoes finds the whole earth leather-covered: contentment transforms every circumstance, which no quantity of outer possessions can do. (2) सन्तोषामृततृप्तानाम्... — the contented enjoy a nectar-like happiness that the wealth-greedy, running hither and thither, never taste: wealth without contentment yields restlessness, not joy. One may add तृष्णाक्षय... — the bliss of ended craving outweighs all worldly and heavenly pleasure. Conclusion: wealth is a means and has real uses, but it satisfies only when governed by contentment; without सन्तोष, acquisition is endless and joyless, and in excess it destroys, as the jackal shows. Hence contentment, which alone converts having into happiness, deserves the name of true wealth.
questions.explanation: Marks for citing two verses accurately, reasoning from them, and a balanced personal conclusion.

questions.question: From the chapter, give four sandhi forms, split each (सन्धि-विच्छेद), and name the type of sandhi involved.
questions.answer: (1) लोभान्मोहः = लोभात् + मोहः — व्यञ्जन-सन्धि (त् → न् before the nasal म्). (2) नाशश्च = नाशः + च — विसर्ग-सन्धि (ः → श् before च). (3) कुतस्तत् = कुतः + तत् — विसर्ग-सन्धि (ः → स् before त्). (4) सुखस्यैते = सुखस्य + एते — वृद्धि-सन्धि (अ + ए = ऐ). Also acceptable: अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य = अतिलोभ + अभिभूतस्य (दीर्घ-सन्धि), इतश्चेतश्च = इतः + च + इतः + च (विसर्ग and गुण sandhis).
questions.explanation: Any four correct examples with splits and named types earn full marks.

questions.question: Survey the case-usage (विभक्ति) of the chapter: for पञ्चमी, तृतीया, षष्ठी and सप्तमी, give one example each from the text with its meaning-role.
questions.answer: पञ्चमी (source, 'from'): लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति — anger arises FROM greed. तृतीया (instrument, 'by/with'): धनुषा जम्बुको हतः — slain BY the bow (also बाणेन, दंष्ट्राभ्याम्). षष्ठी (relation, 'of'): लोभः पापस्य कारणम् — the cause OF sin (also धनुषः कोटिः). सप्तमी (location, 'in/on'): यच्च कामसुखं लोके — pleasure IN the world (also भूमौ, स्कन्धे, मार्गे). Each case ending thus signals the word's role: source, instrument, relation and location respectively.
questions.explanation: One correct example per case with its role earns a mark each.

questions.question: Write a character sketch of the jackal. What do his reasoning, his verse and his death together reveal about the psychology of greed?
questions.answer: The jackal is intelligent but his intelligence is enslaved by greed. Starving, he shows self-restraint — but of a perverted kind: restraint in the service of hoarding, not of wisdom. His calculation verse (मासमेकं नरो याति...) shows a mind that has turned a windfall into an accounting problem: he measures the corpses in months of supply and grudges himself even one honest meal. His choice of the bow-string — the most worthless item — reveals greed's characteristic inversion of values: saving the valuable becomes more important than living well now. His death completes the picture: the bow he was 'economising' kills him, showing that greed is not merely unproductive but self-destructive. The psychology revealed: greed postpones all enjoyment to an imagined future, mistakes accumulation for security, silences present good sense, and finally turns one's own possessions into instruments of ruin.
questions.explanation: The sketch should integrate all three elements: the reasoning, the verse and the manner of death.

questions.question: Compose five simple Sanskrit sentences (in Devanagari) on लोभ and सन्तोष, using vocabulary from the chapter, and give the English meaning of each.
questions.answer: 1. लोभः महान् रिपुः अस्ति। (Greed is a great enemy.) 2. लोभात् नाशः भवति। (From greed comes ruin.) 3. लुब्धः जम्बुकः धनुषा हतः। (The greedy jackal was slain by the bow.) 4. सन्तुष्टः जनः सुखं लभते। (A contented person obtains happiness.) 5. अतिलोभं सर्वदा त्यजेत्। (One should always abandon excessive greed.) — Any five grammatical sentences using chapter vocabulary (लोभ, सन्तोष, जम्बुक, धनुः, नाश, सुख etc.) are acceptable.
questions.explanation: Assess subject-verb agreement, correct vibhakti (e.g. लोभात् पञ्चमी, धनुषा तृतीया) and relevance to the theme.

questions.question: Show how the verse 'लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति...' is enacted step by step in the events of the jackal fable.
questions.answer: The verse names greed's offspring: काम, क्रोध, मोह, नाश. In the fable: (1) काम/लोभ — the jackal's first sight of the bodies kindles not simple hunger but the desire to possess it all for months. (2) मोह (delusion) — greed clouds his judgement: he convinces himself that the wise course is to eat the worthless bow-string and 'save' the meat, a plainly senseless plan dressed up as prudence. (3) The suppressed appetite and anxious hoarding are greed's inner disturbance — the restlessness the सन्तोष verse calls इतश्चेतश्च धावताम्. (4) नाश (ruin) — the deluded choice kills him: the bow pierces his palate. Thus the fable is the verse in motion: greed breeds delusion, delusion breeds the fatal act, and ruin completes the chain — लोभः पापस्य (and here विनाशस्य) कारणम्।
questions.explanation: Marks for mapping each element of the verse's chain onto a concrete event of the story.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer:
'पुरा कस्मिंश्चित् वने एकः व्याधः वसति स्म। एकदा सः मृगयार्थं धनुर्बाणं गृहीत्वा वनं गतः। तत्र सः एकं पुष्टं मृगं बाणेन हतवान्।'
(a) Who lived in the forest? (b) Why did he go into the forest, and what did he take? (c) What did he do there?
questions.answer: (a) A hunter (व्याधः) lived in the forest region. (b) He went for hunting (मृगयार्थम्), taking his bow and arrows (धनुर्बाणम्). (c) There he killed a plump deer (पुष्टं मृगम्) with an arrow.
questions.explanation: मृगयार्थम् = 'for the sake of hunting'; गृहीत्वा = 'having taken' (क्त्वा form).

questions.question:
Read the jackal's verse and answer:
'मासमेकं नरो याति द्वौ मासौ मृगसूकरौ ।
अहिरेकं दिनं याति अद्य भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः ॥'
(a) Who speaks this verse and when? (b) What ration does he assign to each item? (c) What does भक्ष्यो धनुर्गुणः mean? (d) What flaw does the whole calculation expose?
questions.answer: (a) The jackal speaks it on finding the dead hunter, deer, boar and snake. (b) The man: one month; the deer and boar together: two months; the snake: one day. (c) 'Today the bow-string is (the thing) to be eaten' — भक्ष्यः is a यत्-कृदन्त, 'fit to be eaten'. (d) Hoarding greed: even amid abundance he grudges himself real food, and this miserly plan leads directly to his death.
questions.explanation: मृगसूकरौ is a द्वन्द्व dual — 'the deer and the boar'.

questions.question:
Read the closing verse and answer:
'अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् ।
अतिलोभाभिभूतस्य धनुषा जम्बुको हतः ॥'
(a) What is prohibited and what is permitted by the first line? (b) Who was slain, by what? (c) What does अभिभूतस्य mean? (d) State the verse's teaching in one sentence.
questions.answer: (a) Prohibited: excessive greed (अतिलोभ); permitted: ordinary desire need not be wholly abandoned (लोभं नैव परित्यजेत्). (b) The jackal (जम्बुकः) was slain by the bow (धनुषा). (c) अभिभूतस्य = 'of one overcome/overpowered' (by excessive greed). (d) Desire within limits is natural, but greed beyond limit destroys the greedy person himself.
questions.explanation: The verse is the fable's own moral, quoted at its close.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
'लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति लोभात् कामः प्रजायते ।
लोभान्मोहश्च नाशश्च लोभः पापस्य कारणम् ॥'
(a) List the four evils said to spring from greed. (b) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of लोभान्मोहश्च. (c) What विभक्ति is लोभात्, and why? (d) Translate the last quarter (लोभः पापस्य कारणम्).
questions.answer: (a) क्रोधः (anger), कामः (desire), मोहः (delusion) and नाशः (ruin). (b) लोभान्मोहश्च = लोभात् + मोहः + च (त् → न् before म्; ः → श् before च). (c) पञ्चमी, because it expresses the source — the evils arise FROM greed. (d) 'Greed is the cause of sin.'
questions.explanation: The verse gives both the moral chain and two neat sandhi/vibhakti test cases.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
'सन्तोषामृततृप्तानां यत्सुखं शान्तचेतसाम् ।
कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम् ॥'
(a) Whose happiness does the verse praise? (b) Whose happiness does it deny, and with what image? (c) A relative works seven days a week chasing bonuses he never enjoys. Apply this verse to advise him.
questions.answer: (a) The happiness of the peaceful-minded (शान्तचेतसाम्) who are satisfied by the nectar of contentment. (b) It denies real happiness to the wealth-greedy (धनलुब्धानाम्), picturing them as running restlessly hither and thither (इतश्चेतश्च धावताम्). (c) Advice: earning is good, but happiness comes from a settled, contented mind, not from endless chasing; unless he sets a limit and enjoys what he has, the running itself will consume the joy the money was meant to buy.
questions.explanation: Application marks require connecting the verse's image of restless running to the relative's situation.

questions.question:
Read the verse and answer:
'सर्वाः सम्पत्तयस्तस्य सन्तुष्टं यस्य मानसम् ।
उपानद्गूढपादस्य ननु चर्मावृतेव भूः ॥'
(a) Who is said to own all riches? (b) Explain the simile of the shoes. (c) What is the अन्वय of the first line?
questions.answer: (a) The person whose mind (मानसम्) is contented (सन्तुष्टम्). (b) For one whose feet are covered by shoes, the whole earth feels covered with leather: cover your own feet and every road is smooth — likewise, make your own mind content and every circumstance feels rich; you need not remake the world. (c) अन्वय: यस्य मानसं सन्तुष्टम् (अस्ति), तस्य सर्वाः सम्पत्तयः (सन्ति)।
questions.explanation: The simile argues from the economy of inner change over outer accumulation.

questions.question:
Read the line and answer the grammar questions:
'कुतस्तद्धनलुब्धानामितश्चेतश्च धावताम्'
(a) Split कुतस्तत्. (b) What समास is धनलुब्ध, with विग्रह? (c) What does इतश्चेतश्च mean, and from what words is it joined?
questions.answer: (a) कुतस्तत् = कुतः + तत् (visarga → स् before त्). (b) धनलुब्ध is a तत्पुरुष compound — विग्रह: धने लुब्धाः, 'greedy about wealth' (सप्तमी-तत्पुरुष). (c) इतश्चेतश्च = इतः + च + इतः + च, meaning 'hither and thither' — describing the restless running of the greedy.
questions.explanation: One dense quarter-verse carries three separate grammar tests.

questions.question:
Read the sentence from the story and answer:
'क्रुद्धः वराहः तीक्ष्णाभ्यां दंष्ट्राभ्यां व्याधम् अहन्।'
(a) Identify the विभक्ति of दंष्ट्राभ्याम् and its role. (b) Identify the विभक्ति of व्याधम् and its role. (c) Translate the sentence.
questions.answer: (a) दंष्ट्राभ्याम् — तृतीया द्विवचन (instrumental dual): 'with his two (sharp) tusks', the instrument. (b) व्याधम् — द्वितीया एकवचन (accusative singular): 'the hunter', the object of the killing. (c) Translation: 'The enraged boar killed the hunter with his two sharp tusks.'
questions.explanation: The dual instrumental in -भ्याम् is the key recognition point.

questions.question:
Read the situation and answer:
During a shortage, a trader buys up all the grain in his town to resell at a huge price. He refuses every fair offer, waiting for prices to rise further; meanwhile the grain rots in his warehouse and he is ruined.
(a) Which character of the fable does the trader repeat, and how? (b) Which exact detail of the fable matches the rotting grain? (c) Which two Sanskrit maxims from the chapter would you quote to him, and why?
questions.answer: (a) The jackal: amid abundance he refuses present, reasonable enjoyment (fair sale) in order to hoard for an imagined greater gain. (b) As the jackal's hoarded meat lay uneaten while he gnawed the bow-string and died, the trader's hoarded grain rots unsold while he waits — the 'saved' wealth itself becomes the loss. (c) अतिलोभो न कर्तव्यो लोभं नैव परित्यजेत् — trade and profit are permitted, but greed beyond limit destroys; and लोभात् क्रोधः प्रभवति... लोभः पापस्य कारणम् — his greed has bred delusion and ruin, exactly as the verse warns. (सन्तोषामृत... may also be quoted for the remedy.)
questions.explanation: Full marks for mapping character, detail and two aptly chosen maxims with reasons.

Read the verse and answer:
'यच्च कामसुखं लोके यच्च दिव्यं महत्सुखम् ।
तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्यैते नार्हतः षोडशीं कलाम् ॥'
(a) Which two kinds of pleasure are weighed in the first line? (b) Against what are they weighed, and what is the verdict? (c) Split सुखस्यैते and name the sandhi. (d) How does this verse complete the chapter's argument against greed?
questions.answer: (a) Worldly pleasure born of desire (कामसुखं लोके) and the great divine/heavenly pleasure (दिव्यं महत्सुखम्). (b) Against the happiness of the destruction of craving (तृष्णाक्षयसुख); verdict: the two together are not worth one-sixteenth part (षोडशीं कलाम्) of it. (c) सुखस्यैते = सुखस्य + एते — वृद्धि-सन्धि (अ + ए = ऐ). (d) It completes the argument by revaluing the goal itself: since even the best fruits of desire are trivial beside the peace of ended craving, greed pursues the wrong prize altogether — the final answer to लोभ is the extinction of तृष्णा।
questions.explanation: The verse moves the argument from greed's dangers to the superior worth of its opposite.
